prompt: A group of 1,000 members uses Sender Keys. One member's phone was compromised last week and the malware has now been removed. Compared with pairwise Double Ratchet sessions, what is the weakness?

options.text: Sender Keys have no forward secrecy at all
options.explanation: Sender chains are KDF chains, so they do have forward secrecy: past message keys cannot be derived.

options.text: The attacker may still be able to derive future messages from stolen sender chain keys until members distribute new sender keys, so recovery is weaker and slower
options.explanation: Correct. Sender Keys have no per-message DH ratchet; healing requires rotating sender keys (for example, when members join or leave).
That is the cost Sender Keys *avoid*. Each message is encrypted once and fanned out by the server.

options.text: The server can read the group messages
options.explanation: Sender keys are distributed over pairwise E2EE sessions, so the server never sees them.

workedExample: A stolen set of sender chain keys lets an attacker compute future keys in those chains; the one-way property protects the erased past, not the future. Recovery requires distributing fresh sender secrets through channels whose security has themselves recovered. Pairwise ratchets and MLS offer different recovery mechanisms, with guarantees conditional on fresh unknown contributions and delivered updates. MLS path length is logarithmic in a favourable populated tree, not a universal bound on all update costs.

link.title: RFC 9420: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol

prompt: Assume a populated balanced tree with no extra resolution overhead. An MLS group has 4,096 members arranged in a TreeKEM binary tree. Roughly how many tree nodes does a member update when refreshing their own key, compared with re-keying pairwise to everyone?

options.text: One, because the group shares a single key
options.explanation: There is one group secret per epoch, but changing it securely needs new keys along the updater's path so that each subtree can decrypt.

options.text: About 64, the square root of the group size
options.explanation: TreeKEM's cost is logarithmic, not square-root.
That is the pairwise cost. The point of the tree is to avoid it.

options.text: About 12 path nodes versus 4,095 pairwise messages
options.explanation: Correct. A balanced binary tree with 4,096 leaves has depth 12 (2 to the power 12 is 4,096), so an update replaces the keys on the path to the root.

workedExample:
1. Leaves are members; each internal node has a key pair known to the members below it.
2. To update, a member picks new secrets for their leaf and every ancestor up to the root.
3. For each node on the path, they encrypt its new secret to the sibling subtree's node key. One ciphertext covers a whole subtree.
4. Path length: see the formula below.
5. Pairwise re-keying would need a message to each of the 4,095 others. (Real trees can be unbalanced or have blank nodes, so costs vary, but stay logarithmic in the good case.)

```formula
L = log_2(N)
L = log_2(4,096) = 12
where
L: the depth of a balanced binary tree: the number of nodes on a member's path that an update refreshes
N: the number of members, one per leaf
log_2: logarithm base 2: the power 2 must be raised to; 2^12 = 4,096
In words: 4,096 is 12 copies of 2 multiplied together, so a balanced tree of 4,096 members is 12 levels deep.
```

This counts the 12 ancestors above the refreshed leaf. The leaf key also changes; real MLS update ciphertexts and work additionally depend on blank nodes and resolutions.

link.title: RFC 9420: The Messaging Layer Security (MLS) Protocol
